newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Stubborn Australia dlr soaks up heavy selling.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Stubborn Australia dlr soaks up heavy selling.

text.p: The Australian dollar bowed beneath heavy offshore selling Wednesday, but had so far found enough local demand to avoid a damaging break of support.

Figures showing some moderation in wages growth also gave reason to pause but analysts emphasised that although promising for low inflation, they were not compelling enough to seriously raise the risk of another rate cut.

"There's been good amounts sold, particularly on AUD/yen and AUD/mark, and the market's still a little long," said one. "But we've also seen decent domestic demand and the dip feels more like a profit-taking correction than a lasting shake out."
Accordingly, he expected US$0.7720 to provide a floor short term while failures at 78 cents made it a formidable ceiling.
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the dollar was making a fight of it at US$0.7749/54 after ducking as deep as US$0.7738 from an early US$0.7756/61 and US$0.7758/63 late here Tuesday.
Traders said offers originated from numerous sources including an aggressive New York investment bank which was believed to have been a big buyer in U.S. time only to turn into a raging seller today.
In contrast, exporters were on the bid and dealers were surprised by the amount of selling soaked up at US$0.7740.
The currency was pressured on the crosses where both it and the US$ ran into heavy Japanese offers, thought to be related to repatriation for their March 31 year-end.
The local unit swayed to 93.62/72 yen from 94.71/81 late Tuesday while the US$/yen dived to 120.90 from 122.10.

Similar losses were notched up on the mark and Swiss franc as investors took the weakness of the U.S. dollar as a cue to realise profits on recent steep gains. That combined to drag the trade weighted index down to 59.1 from a 59.3 close Tuesday.
Today's wages data also prompted some initial sales, but the impact faded quickly when the market took a closer look.

Private sector enterprise pay deals slowed to an average annualised 4.4 percent in the December quarter from 5.3 percent the quarter before, while growth for all sectors moderated to 4.4 percent from 4.8 percent.
That boded well for keeping inflation contained, but most analysts felt the economic outlook was robust enough that the Reserve Bank would not want to ease policy anyway.

"The RBA itself is very upbeat on the growth outlook and we believe it has every reason to be," said Andrew Ticehurst, an economist at Macquarie Bank. "The economic data will have to be very weak in the next few months to change that."
"It doesn't change our view on monetary policy which is that the chance of another official cut is very low," he said.
A much broader measure of wages is due Thursday in the shape of Q4 average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE).

These originally showed a higher than expected 1.2 percent gain on the quarter and 3.9 percent rise year-on-year, and analysts noted data from the previous two quarters were revised up in their final release.
The figures will also include a breakdown between public and private sector wages, and analysts were interested to see if they showed the same moderation as the enterprise measure.
